analysis.research_question_and_background: This study investigates the durability of immunity and safety of RSV vaccination in high-risk transplant recipients, addressing the need for effective prevention strategies in populations vulnerable to severe RSV disease.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A nonrandomized clinical trial was conducted among recipients of lung transplant and allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant to evaluate humoral and cell-mediated immunity and longer-term safety following RSV vaccination.
analysis.methods: The study employed a nonrandomized design to assess immune responses and safety outcomes through clinical evaluation and immunological assays, focusing on vaccine-induced immunity in transplant recipients.
analysis.main_results: The study directly observed the safety profile and immune response durability following RSV vaccination in high-risk transplant recipients, though specific numerical results are not detailed in the abstract.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that RSV vaccination may be safe and induce durable immunity in high-risk transplant recipients, offering novel insights into vaccine efficacy in this vulnerable population.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results inform the potential use of RSV vaccines in high-risk transplant recipients, contributing to strategies for preventing severe RSV disease in immunocompromised individuals.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is nonrandomized, which may introduce bias, and the abstract does not provide detailed statistical or numerical outcomes, limiting the strength of the evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the durability of immunity and safety of RSV vaccination in high-risk transplant recipients, focusing on lung and allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant patients. The nonrandomized clinical trial examines humoral and cell-mediated immune responses following vaccination, highlighting the potential for RSV vaccines to prevent severe disease in immunocompromised individuals. While the findings suggest vaccine safety and immune response durability, the study's nonrandomized design and lack of detailed numerical results limit the strength of the evidence. The results contribute to understanding the role of vaccination in protecting transplant recipients from RSV, informing future research and public health strategies for this vulnerable group.

papers.title_zh: 免疫持续性和RSV 疫苗接种在高风险移植受者的安全性
papers.source_body_en: This nonrandomized clinical trial examines humoral and cell-mediated immunity and longer-term safety following vaccination for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) among recipients of lung transplant and allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant.
papers.abstract_zh: 这项非随机临床试验评估了在肺移植和异基因造血细胞移植受者中接受疫苗接种(RSV)后体液免疫和细胞介导免疫的持续性以及长期安全性。
papers.summary_zh: 这项非随机临床试验评估了在肺移植和异基因造血细胞移植受者中接受疫苗接种(RSV)后体液免疫和细胞介导免疫的持续性以及长期安全性。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究探讨了RSV 疫苗接种在高风险移植受者中的免疫持续性和安全性,旨在解决免疫功能低下人群中有效预防策略的需求。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 在肺移植和异基因造血细胞移植受者中开展了一项非随机临床试验,以评估接受RSV 疫苗接种后的体液免疫和细胞介导免疫以及长期安全性。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究采用非随机设计,通过临床评估和免疫学检测来评估免疫应答的安全性和免疫应答,重点关注疫苗在移植受者中诱导的免疫应答。
analysis_zh.main_results: 研究直接观察了RSV 疫苗接种在高风险移植受者中诱导的免疫持续性和安全性,但摘要中未详细列出具体数值结果。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,RSV 疫苗接种可能在高风险移植受者中是安全的,并能诱导持久的免疫应答,为这一易感人群中的疫苗有效性提供了新的见解。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为RSV 疫苗在高风险移植受者中的潜在应用提供了依据,有助于制定针对免疫功能低下人群预防严重RSV疾病的策略。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究为非随机设计,可能引入偏倚,且摘要中未提供详细的统计或数值结果,限制了证据的强度。

To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk. Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/respiratory-syncytial-virus-rsv-maternal-vaccination-coverage-in-england/respiratory-syncytial-virus-rsv-maternal-vaccination-coverage-in-england-june-2026-report Published 5 November 2026 This report presents monthly vaccine uptake data for the maternal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunisation programme in England, focusing on the period up to June 2026. It includes vaccine uptake estimates for pregnant women who delivered in June 2026 following the introduction of the RSV maternal vaccination programme in September 2024. Main points The main messages of this report are: 62.0% (26,252 out of 42,326) of women who reported giving birth during the reporting month received an RSV vaccine uptake varied by NHS commissioning region, with the highest uptake reported in the South West region (71.9%) and the lowest in the London region (54.6%) uptake varied across integrated care boards (ICBs), with the highest uptake reported in the Dorset ICB (76.0%) and the lowest in Birmingham and Solihull ICB (39.5%) uptake varied across local authorities, with the highest uptake reported in West Berkshire (86.6%) and the lowest in Enfield (34.5%) uptake varied by ethnic group, with the highest uptake reported among the Asian or Asian British - Chinese ethnic group (75.0%), and the lowest among the Black - Caribbean ethnic group (35.4%) Help us improve this resource This vaccine uptake report has been designated as an official statistics release. As part of this process, we are seeking feedback from users to ensure the publication meets your needs. We would be grateful if you could take a few minutes to complete a short survey and share your views. Please complete the survey Your input will play an important role in shaping the development of this publication. Thank you for your time and support. Analysis of maternal RSV vaccine uptake Maternal uptake of the RSV vaccine is assessed monthly to monitor the reach and impact of the national immunisation programme. Given the programme’s design, uptake is defined as the proportion of pregnant women who delivered in the reporting month and had received the RSV vaccine during pregnancy. This metric serves as a proxy for vaccine coverage by infant birth month, reflecting the extent of passive immunity conferred to newborns. This monthly report presents RSV vaccine uptake for women who delivered in June 2026, 22 months after the start of the RSV vaccination programme. The monthly uptake trend among pregnant women who have delivered since the programme’s launch is presented in Figure 1. Overall, the monthly RSV maternal vaccine uptake for June 2026 was 62.0%. RSV uptake increased in the first few months of the programme and has remained steady since October 2025. Figure 1. RSV vaccine uptake (%) trend among pregnant women by month of delivery, September 2024 to June 2026 Note 1: the vertical lines represent a change in the percentage of GP (general practitioner) practices used to calculate RSV vaccine uptake. Up to December 2024, vaccine uptake was estimated based on data from a single supplier covering fewer than 40.5% of GP practices. From January 2025 onwards, vaccine uptake was based on data from more than 97.5% of GP practices and is more representative of national vaccination uptake. This month’s report includes data from both major GP IT suppliers, substantially expanding the data available in the earliest reports (September to December 2024). It includes data from 98.6% of GPs in England, up from 40.4% of participating GPs during the first 4 months (September to December 2024) of the vaccination programme. This has been made possible by improvements in data quality and permits a more representative analysis of uptake and trends across England. To further explore variation in uptake, Table 1 presents uptake by commissioning region, while Table 2 provides the breakdown by ethnicity. As shown in Table 1, there are notable regional differences in uptake, with variation of up to 17.3 percentage points between NHS commissioning regions. Table 1. RSV vaccine uptake (%) in pregnant women, measured in June 2026, by NHS commissioning region Change to table view Commissioning region RSV uptake (%) North East and Yorkshire 62.9 North West 59.2 Midlands 58.5 East of England 64.0 London 54.6 South East 68.8 South West 71.9 Commissioning region RSV uptake (%) North East and Yorkshire 62.9 North West 59.2 Midlands 58.5 East of England 64.0 London 54.6 South East 68.8 South West 71.9 Variation in uptake by ethnicity was also observed, with a gap of 39.6 percentage points observed in the uptake between ethnic groups (Table 2). Table 2. RSV vaccine uptake (%) in pregnant women, measured in June 2026, by ethnicity Change to table view Ethnic group [note 2] RSV uptake (%) Asian or Asian British - any other Asian background 64.9 Asian or Asian British - Bangladeshi 53.7 Asian or Asian British - Chinese 75.0 Asian or Asian British - Indian 72.9 Asian or Asian British - Pakistani 42.6 Black or Black British - African 49.1 Black or Black British - any other Black background 51.9 Black or Black British - Caribbean 35.4 Mixed - any other mixed background 61.1 Mixed - White and Asian 55.8 Mixed - White and Black African 54.9 Mixed - White and Black Caribbean 43.3 White - British 68.5 White - Irish 64.1 White - any other White background 49.5 Any other ethnicity code 62.2 Ethnicity - unknown 55.0 Other ethnic group - any other ethnic group 49.5 Ethnic group [note 2] RSV uptake (%) Asian or Asian British - any other Asian background 64.9 Asian or Asian British - Bangladeshi 53.7 Asian or Asian British - Chinese 75.0 Asian or Asian British - Indian 72.9 Asian or Asian British - Pakistani 42.6 Black or Black British - African 49.1 Black or Black British - any other Black background 51.9 Black or Black British - Caribbean 35.4 Mixed - any other mixed background 61.1 Mixed - White and Asian 55.8 Mixed - White and Black African 54.9 Mixed - White and Black Caribbean 43.3 White - British 68.5 White - Irish 64.1 White - any other White background 49.5 Any other ethnicity code 62.2 Ethnicity - unknown 55.0 Other ethnic group - any other ethnic group 49.5 Note 2: the ‘Ethnicity - unknown’ group combines all records where ethnicity was not provided. This includes people whose ethnicity was not recorded, not stated, or who refused to give their ethnicity. The ‘Any other ethnicity code’ category includes individuals whose ethnicity has been recorded using non-standard or legacy codes (that is, codes not aligned with the 2001 or 2011 Census classifications). The map in Figure 2 shows RSV uptake by ICB. Uptake varied across ICBs by 36.5 percentage points with the highest uptake reported in Dorset (76.0) and the lowest uptake reported in Birmingham and Solihull (39.5). Figure 2. RSV vaccine uptake (%) among pregnant women delivering in June 2026, by ICB Across the local authorities, uptake differed by 52.1 percentage points with the highest uptake reported in West Berkshire (86.6%) and the lowest uptake reported in Enfield (34.5%). The variation across the local authorities is presented in the map shown in Figure 3. Figure 3. RSV vaccine uptake (%) among pregnant women delivering in June 2026, by local authority Further detail, including uptake figures broken down by local authority and ICB, can be found in the June 2026 supplementary data tables. Since the RSV maternal vaccination programme has now been running for 22 months (up to the reporting month), an increasing number of pregnant women are receiving the vaccine during their eligible window. This growing awareness and notification from gestation week 20 onwards have contributed to a gradual increase in monthly vaccine uptake from 40.5% in September 2024 to the current figure reported for June 2026. As the programme continues and more women are informed earlier in their pregnancies, monthly vaccination uptake is expected to gradually increase. Data sources and methodology Further details on the data sources, methodology, data quality, and limitations are available in the quality and methodology information (QMI) report. The maternal RSV vaccine coverage estimates are calculated using monthly GP practice data automatically submitted to ImmForm by participating GP IT suppliers and validated and analysed by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). The report covers women who delivered during the reporting month (1 June 2026 to 30 June 2026), excluding miscarriages and stillbirths, with uptake measured as receipt of RSV vaccination from 28 weeks of pregnancy up to delivery. To ensure complete and accurate recording of vaccination and delivery information, data are extracted using a three-month reporting lag. The June 2026 estimates are based on data from the two major GP IT suppliers, representing 98.6% of participating GP practices nationally. The July 2026 maternal RSV vaccination uptake report is scheduled to be released on 3 December 2026. Background information The RSV vaccine has been offered to pregnant women in England since September 2024 to address the significant burden of RSV-related illness, hospitalisations and deaths, particularly among infants under six months of age and older adults, who are at increased risk of lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) (see the Green Book on immunisation). In 2023, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) issued a full statement recommending the implementation of a maternal RSV vaccination programme. This recommendation was based on robust evidence demonstrating the safety and effectiveness of RSV vaccines in protecting infants during their most vulnerable period. The vaccine is recommended as a year-round programme to be administered from 28 weeks of gestation onwards. This timing aligns with the optimal window for passive antibody transfer to the foetus, ensuring effective protection against severe RSV-related illness. From 1 September 2024 (the programme start date), all women who are at least 28 weeks pregnant are advised to receive the vaccine as soon as possible, with vaccination continuing to be recommended for all eligible women throughout pregnancy up until delivery. Additionally, the vaccine will be reoffered for every subsequent pregnancy to maintain consistent coverage and protection. This monthly report includes vaccine uptake data for women who delivered in June 2026. Programme delivery The programme is delivered through GP and maternity services, ensuring accessible vaccination opportunities for eligible pregnant women across England. In addition, the RSV vaccine is available through the community pharmacy delivery model at approximately 37 sites across two ICBs in the East of England. It is also available at up to 200 additional community pharmacy sites across the Midlands, North West, and London commissioning regions during the 2025 to 2026 expansion phase. Previous monthly reports are available at RSV maternal vaccination coverage in England. news.title_zh: 2026年6月 呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)产妇 疫苗接种 覆盖情况报告 - GOV.UK
news.source_body_en: The June 2026 report from the UK Health Security Agency provides an update on the maternal RSV vaccination programme in England, which began in September 2024. The report highlights that 62.0% of women who delivered in June 2026 received the RSV vaccine during pregnancy. This uptake varied significantly by NHS commissioning region, with the South West region reporting the highest uptake at 71.9% and London the lowest at 54.6%. Additionally, uptake differed by integrated care board (ICB), ranging from 76.0% in Dorset to 39.5% in Birmingham and Solihull. Ethnic disparities were also noted, with the Asian or Asian British - Chinese group having the highest uptake at 75.0% and the Black - Caribbean group the lowest at 35.4%. The data is based on information from over 97.5% of GP practices since January 2025, reflecting improved data quality and a more representative analysis of the programme's reach. The report serves as an official statistics release and aims to monitor the impact of the national immunisation programme in reducing the burden of RSV-related illness, hospitalisations, and deaths, especially among infants under six months and older adults.
news.content_zh: 英国卫生安全局2026年6月的报告提供了英格兰自2024年9月启动的产妇RSV 疫苗接种计划的最新进展。报告指出,2026年6月分娩的女性中,有62.0%在孕期接受了RSV 疫苗。该接种率在NHS委托地区间存在显著差异,西南地区报告最高接种率为71.9%,而伦敦最低为54.6%。此外,接种率在整合照护委员会(ICB)间也有所不同,从多塞特的76.0%到伯明翰和索利赫尔的39.5%。种族差异也有所体现,亚洲或亚洲英国-中国群体的接种率最高,为75.0%,而黑人-加勒比群体最低,为35.4%。数据基于自2025年1月以来超过97.5%的全科医生(GP)诊所的信息,反映了数据质量的提升以及对计划覆盖范围更具代表性的分析。该报告作为官方统计数据发布,旨在监测全国疫苗接种计划对降低RSV相关疾病、住院和死亡负担的影响,尤其是对6个月以下婴儿和老年人群的影响。

news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-5-november-2026-week-45 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. The report is based on data up to week 44 of 2026 (26 October to 1 November 2026). The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity showed variable trends across surveillance indicators and is circulating at low levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) increased slightly and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. A briefing note has been issued to inform the NHS that influenza activity is now above baseline levels. Influenza vaccination data was unavailable or incomplete at the time of analysis in weeks 41 and 42 and led to several cohorts not being published in week 42. This has been corrected since week 43, and all cohorts are included. This will be corrected retrospectively in the report for week 42. There remains an issue that affects the attribution of vaccinations by provider setting. The correct identification of vaccinations administered in pharmacies cannot currently be reliably distinguished from those administered in general practices or other healthcare settings. As a result, some pharmacy vaccinations are likely to be misclassified as general practice or other healthcare settings, artificially increasing vaccination activity reported for general practices and other healthcare settings and reducing activity reported for pharmacies. This is not expected to affect overall vaccination uptake estimates, which are considered to remain an accurate reflection of the influenza vaccination programme. Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 44 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (59.1% vs 61.5%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (27.9% vs 28.9%), those aged 2 years (33.3% vs 34.2%), and those aged 3 years (33.1% vs 34.3%). In contrast, vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (31.1% vs 29.7%). COVID-19 activity decreased and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness remained stable. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 5 November 2026 (week 45) provides an overview of respiratory virus activity in England. The report is based on data up to week 44 (26 October to 1 November 2026) and highlights that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) activity increased, circulating at baseline levels. Emergency department attendances for acute bronchiolitis rose but remained within seasonally expected ranges. The report also notes that influenza activity showed variable trends, with ED attendances for influenza-like illness slightly above seasonally expected levels. Influenza A positivity increased, while influenza B remained stable. The report acknowledges data quality issues, particularly in vaccine uptake reporting, and mentions that some pharmacy vaccinations may be misclassified. It does not provide specific case counts or risk levels for RSV, focusing instead on surveillance trends and methodological considerations.

She joined Britannica in 2006 and... Kara Rogers Fact-checked by Britannica Editors Encyclopaedia Britannica's editors oversee subject areas in which they have extensive knowledge, whether from years of experience gained by working on that content or via study for an advanced degree.... Britannica Editors Last updated Nov. 8, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything News • Medical societies unify to endorse evidence-based respiratory vaccine guidance • Nov. 5, 2026, 2:39 PM ET (News-Medical) ...(Show more) Cranking up a natural defense pathway boosts cells' resistance to RSV • Oct. 20, 2026, 12:40 PM ET (Medical Xpress) Show less respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), infectious agent of the respiratory system that typically produces a mild coldlike illness but in susceptible individuals, particularly infants under six months of age, is a major cause of severe and potentially fatal lower respiratory disease. Severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) occurs most commonly in the elderly and in young children. An estimated 60 to 70 percent of children have been infected with RSV by age one, and nearly all children have been infected by age two. Because RSV effectively evades immunity, repeat infections are common. RSV infection is seasonal, occurring as an annual epidemic during the winter in most countries in temperate regions. What's the Difference Between Bacteria and Viruses?Knowing the difference isn't just a technical distinction—it can save lives.(more) See all videos for this article Direct person-to-person contact is thought to be the most common route of RSV transmission. The virus also can be transmitted through the air, such as by coughing or sneezing, and through direct contact with a contaminated surface followed by touching of the face. Symptoms generally appear within four to six days of infection and include runny nose, cough, sore throat, headache, fever, and wheezing. In instances of severe illness, affected individuals may have a high fever, severe wheezing, rapid or laboured breathing, and bluish lips or fingers. Infants may only show signs of irritability, fatigue, and breathing difficulties, even in severe cases. The only pharmacological therapy available for treatment of RSV is the nucleoside analogue ribavirin, which can be administered orally, parenterally (by injection or infusion), or by inhalation. An injectable humanized monoclonal antibody is available for prevention of severe RSV illness in high-risk infants and children. It provides passive immunity and must by given by intramuscular injection once a month during RSV season. Transmission can be prevented with frequent handwashing, cleaning of surfaces, avoiding close contact with others, and covering the mouth and nose with the upper arm when coughing or sneezing. Kara Rogers Fact-checked by Britannica Editors Encyclopaedia Britannica's editors oversee subject areas in which they have extensive knowledge, whether from years of experience gained by working on that content or via study for an advanced degree.... Britannica Editors Last updated Nov. 8, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything News • Medical societies unify to endorse evidence-based respiratory vaccine guidance • Nov. 5, 2026, 2:39 PM ET (News-Medical) ...(Show more) Cranking up a natural defense pathway boosts cells' resistance to RSV • Oct. 20, 2026, 12:40 PM ET (Medical Xpress) Show less respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), infectious agent of the respiratory system that typically produces a mild coldlike illness but in susceptible individuals, particularly infants under six months of age, is a major cause of severe and potentially fatal lower respiratory disease. Severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) occurs most commonly in the elderly and in young children. An estimated 60 to 70 percent of children have been infected with RSV by age one, and nearly all children have been infected by age two. Because RSV effectively evades immunity, repeat infections are common. RSV infection is seasonal, occurring as an annual epidemic during the winter in most countries in temperate regions. What's the Difference Between Bacteria and Viruses?Knowing the difference isn't just a technical distinction—it can save lives.(more) See all videos for this article Direct person-to-person contact is thought to be the most common route of RSV transmission. The virus also can be transmitted through the air, such as by coughing or sneezing, and through direct contact with a contaminated surface followed by touching of the face. Symptoms generally appear within four to six days of infection and include runny nose, cough, sore throat, headache, fever, and wheezing. In instances of severe illness, affected individuals may have a high fever, severe wheezing, rapid or laboured breathing, and bluish lips or fingers. Infants may only show signs of irritability, fatigue, and breathing difficulties, even in severe cases. The only pharmacological therapy available for treatment of RSV is the nucleoside analogue ribavirin, which can be administered orally, parenterally (by injection or infusion), or by inhalation. An injectable humanized monoclonal antibody is available for prevention of severe RSV illness in high-risk infants and children. It provides passive immunity and must by given by intramuscular injection once a month during RSV season. Transmission can be prevented with frequent handwashing, cleaning of surfaces, avoiding close contact with others, and covering the mouth and nose with the upper arm when coughing or sneezing. (Albany, New York) - November 10, 2026: DelveInsight's "Respiratory Syncytial Virus Market Insights, Epidemiology, and Market Forecast-2034 report offers an in-depth understanding of the Respiratory Syncytial Virus, historical and forecasted epidemiology as well as the Respiratory Syncytial Virus market trends in the United States, EU4 (Germany, Spain, Italy, France) the United Kingdom and Japan. To Know in detail about the Respiratory Syncytial Virus market outlook, drug uptake, treatment scenario and epidemiology trends, Click here; Respiratory Syncytial Virus Market Forecast [https://www.delveinsight.com/sample-request/respiratory-syncytial-virus-rsv-market?utm_source=abnewswire&utm_medium=pressrelease&utm_campaign=gaurav] Some of the key facts of the Respiratory Syncytial Virus Market Report: * The Respiratory Syncytial Virus market size was valued approximately USD 1,300 million in 2023 and is anticipated to grow with a significant CAGR during the study period (2020-2034). * In October 2026, Enanta Pharmaceuticals announced that the first patient had been dosed in the RESOLVE Phase IIb/III clinical trial evaluating zelicapavir in adults at high risk of severe RSV outcomes. * In October 2026, A Phase II clinical study evaluating Moderna's investigational mRNA-1345 RSV vaccine in children aged 2 to under 18 years was published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases on October 17, 2026. The trial assessed the vaccine's safety, reactogenicity, and immunogenicity in healthy children and those at increased risk of RSV infection. Among the 346 vaccinated participants, mRNA-1345 demonstrated a favorable safety profile and elicited strong neutralizing antibody responses against both RSV-A and RSV-B. Critics point out that national-level preventive management measures are urgently needed for the elderly as there is a high risk of leading to fatal serious complications such as pneumonia or worsening of underlying diseases in case of infection. According to the Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on the 3rd, the number of people aged 65 or older hospitalized with RSV infection in Korea has continued to increase sharply every year from 433 in 2022 to 1,130 in 2023 and 2032 in 2024. In particular, as of the 3rd of last month (week 40), when the full-fledged epidemic began, the number of patients has already reached 3,300 this year, 1.7 times the total number of patients (1906) last year. The number of patients as well as changes in composition ratio by age are clear. Of the total inpatients (6710) this year, 49.2% of those aged 65 or older accounted for half. Considering that it was only 5.2% in 2022, it shows that the burden of disease from RSV infection has been rapidly shifting from infants to the elderly in recent years. Experts warn that RSV infection in the elderly is at high risk of being directly linked to severe disease. This is because the virus' defense has declined due to immune aging that occurs with age. In addition, lung function and weakened respiratory muscles reduce the ability to spit out airway secretions such as phlegm, making them more vulnerable to infection. According to a study published in the international journal Scientific Report by a team of professors at Korea University Ansan Hospital, 56.8% of RSV hospitalized patients aged 65 or older in Korea were accompanied by pneumonia, and 25% were transferred to intensive care units. Their in-hospital mortality rate reached 10.6%. It is even more fatal for the elderly with underlying diseases. According to an analysis of RSV hospitalized patients aged 60 or older published in the international journal Journal of Infection Digits, 80% of COPD patients, 38% of heart failure patients, and 50% of asthma patients had worsened symptoms of the existing disease during inpatient treatment. In a study of 471 inpatients in the United States, new cardiovascular adverse reactions such as heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and myocardial infarction were identified in 37%. "Korea has limited adult RSV diagnostic tests and relies on a sample monitoring system, so it is easy to underestimate the actual disease burden of high-risk groups," said Park Jin-joo, a professor of circulatory medicine at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. "We need to upgrade the monitoring system so that we can accurately grasp the overall disease burden and actively inform patients and their guardians of the risk of infection and the need for vaccination." The burden of disease continues for a long time even after acute treatment is over. According to the international academic journal 'Influenza and Arthur's Respiracy Virus', 33% of RSV hospitalized patients aged 60 or older lost their ability to perform daily life such as eating and bathing even six months after discharge, and 38.3% were readmitted within six months. 14% of discharged patients required a higher level of care and care than before admission. RSV, along with flu and COVID-19, is classified as a level 4 legal infectious disease that can be prevented by vaccines. However, the national infectious disease management system still has a wide gap. While the government provides free national vaccination (NIP) for the elderly aged 65 or older in the case of influenza and COVID-19, RSV still focuses only on hygiene management centered on infants and postpartum care centers and childcare facilities. Medical guidelines already specify vaccinations for the elderly. Major domestic and foreign institutions, including the Korean Infectious Society and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recommend a single dose of RSV vaccine for all adults over the age of 75 and high-risk groups aged 50 to 74 who suffer from chronic diseases or immunocompromised diseases. On the other hand, discussions on introducing domestic NIPs to ensure their access to vaccines have not even taken the first step. RSV infection in the elderly also leads to enormous socioeconomic losses. The international journal 'Journal of Virology' estimated that the total annual medical expenses related to RSV for the elderly exceed 1.48 trillion won. Another academic journal, "Pharmaco Economics Open," also analyzed that an average of 9.37 million won and 10.4 days of hospitalization for RSV infection are required. Experts point out that the burden of such diseases can be substantially relieved through vaccination. According to the international journal "Human Vaccine and ImmunoCeraputics", if people aged 60 or older receive RSV vaccines, direct and indirect costs such as treatment costs and productivity losses are expected to be reduced by a total of 20.675 trillion won. The loss of QALY, an indicator that reflects the deterioration of quality of life due to disease, can also be reduced by 244,424 years. Major overseas countries tend to recognize the cost-effectiveness of vaccines and quickly provide public support. Following the recommendation of vaccination for senior citizens aged 75 to 79, the UK has gradually expanded the scope of support to residents of nursing homes aged 80 or older and those aged 65 to 74 with underlying diseases this year. Australia also provides NIP to those aged 75 or older in consideration of the risk of hospitalization by age, and provides vaccination to indigenous Australians who have a relatively early risk of disease burden from the age of 60. In addition, Canada, Germany, and the United States are continuing to support vaccination for high-risk groups through public health insurance or state programs. Professor Park said, "It is time for Korea to discuss the introduction of NIP by comprehensively evaluating the burden of RSV disease, prevention effect, and cost-effectiveness of vaccines due to aging." supplementary_news.content: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody that provides season-long protection against RSV in infants, reducing medically attended infections and hospitalizations. Maternal vaccination and nirsevimab together offer complementary strategies to protect newborns during their highest-risk months. Overview Feature Articles Latest Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) News and Research Early-infancy infection with RSV increases the risk of developing childhood asthma Belgian scientists from VIB and Ghent University (UGent), together with Danish collaborators, have uncovered compelling evidence that early-infancy infection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) significantly increases the risk of developing childhood asthma-especially in children with a family history of allergy or asthma. Year-round access to RSV immunization may reduce major seasonal outbreaks Providing year-round access to RSV immunization would minimize the risk of large seasonal outbreaks across the nation, including in both urban and rural areas. Preparing for the respiratory virus season: A guide for families As respiratory virus season begins, pediatric experts are preparing for an expected rise in cases of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which can cause cold-like symptoms in most people but serious illness in infants and older adults. COVID-19, RSV, and flu vaccines remain safe and effective The systematic review provides crucial insights into the efficacy and safety of respiratory virus vaccines, supporting evidence-based immunization practices. Study reveals impact of viral combinations on infant respiratory illness severity A new study led by researchers at National Jewish Health has revealed that, while a wide range of viruses can cause lower respiratory tract illnesses (LRIs) in infants, certain viruses and viral combinations dramatically increase the risk of severe disease. A parent's guide to manage pediatric respiratory illnesses during the virus season As we head deeper into fall and toward the holiday season, your little one may start to exhibit symptoms like a runny nose, cough, or fever. HEPA purifiers do not fully reduce classroom viral exposure In a secondary analysis of a study of 200 classrooms, Mass General Brigham researchers found respiratory viral exposures were still high in those with HEPA purifiers, suggesting additional interventions are needed. RSV vaccines protect two most-at-risk groups from severe illness The review demonstrates that vaccines for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are both safe and effective in protecting groups who are most at risk for serious illness, including older adults and infants. Soap shortages undermine global hand hygiene efforts A lack of soap is the most often reported barrier to effective hand hygiene-key to curbing the spread of infection-in shared community spaces, such as households, schools, and public places, finds a systematic review of the available research, published in the open access journal BMJ Global Health. RSV vaccine slashes hospitalizations in older adults in real-world trial A large, real-world randomized trial in Denmark found that the RSVpreF vaccine reduced RSV-related hospitalizations in adults aged 60 and over by over 80%. The vaccine also showed protection against broader respiratory illness with a favorable safety profile. Healthy newborns also face high risk of severe RSV infection It is not only premature babies and children with underlying diseases who suffer from serious respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections. Can an allergy spray help prevent COVID-19? Researchers determine the efficacy and safety of azelastine nasal spray for preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthy adults. How effective is the RSV vaccine for older adults? A single dose of the RSV vaccine offers 58% protection against hospitalization in older adults, but effectiveness varies in immunocompromised individuals. New guidelines improve care for respiratory infections in leukemia patients People with leukemia have a weakened immune system due to the disease itself and treatment, which leads to an increased susceptibility to infections. RSV causes severe outcomes and heart complications in older adults Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a well-known cause of infections in children, but it's understudied in older individuals. Maternal RSV vaccination linked to sharp drop in infant lung infections Vaccination of pregnant women has been linked to a drop in newborns being admitted to hospital with a serious lung infection, research suggests. Light-activated drug discovery identifies broad-spectrum antivirals UC Santa Barbara researchers and collaborators from campus biotech spinoff Integrated Biosciences, as well as Harvard, MIT and genomics company Illumina Ventures are using optogenetics - the use of light to probe the functions of living tissue - to find compounds to help our bodies more effectively help themselves in times of physiological stress. How underreporting masks the real impact of RSV in older populations Research shows RSV leads to high hospitalization rates in adults, emphasizing the importance of enhanced surveillance and diagnostic measures in healthcare. New RSV guideline aims to standardize pediatric care across China Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections (ALRTIs) in children under five and poses a persistent threat to child health worldwide. WHO releases first-ever position paper on immunization products to protect infants against RSV Today, the World Health Organization (WHO) published its first-ever position paper on immunization products to protect infants against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – the leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in children globally

supplementary_news.content_title: Subconjunctival Hemorrhage and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection in an Infant Evaluated for Non-accidental Trauma: A Case Report of a Possible Association
supplementary_news.content: Abstract A six-week-old previously healthy infant was found to have a subconjunctival hemorrhage (SCH) and concomitant respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. Because SCH in an infant may represent a sentinel finding of non-accidental trauma (NAT), an extensive multidisciplinary evaluation was performed, which identified no traumatic injuries or evidence of abuse. The SCH resolved within one week, and the patient recovered with supportive care without complications. To our knowledge, SCH in association with RSV has not previously been reported, despite RSV being common in infants. As with SCH reported in association with other respiratory infections, inflammatory and pressure-related processes are possible mechanisms, although this observational case cannot establish causation. Reporting this possible association may broaden the differential diagnosis of SCH to include other medical causes in infants with RSV, while reinforcing the need for completing a thorough screening for abuse. Identifying medical causes for childhood injuries is as important as accurately diagnosing inflicted injury, as misdiagnosing child abuse can have serious medicolegal consequences for children and their families. Introduction Subconjunctival hemorrhage (SCH) is a sentinel finding of pediatric non-accidental trauma (NAT), and SCH remains an important and well-documented extraocular manifestation of NAT [1]. However, pediatric SCH has multiple reported age-dependent etiologies such as trauma, Valsalva associated with coughing/vomiting, coagulopathy, and infection, which may overlap with NAT as an etiology. Often, isolated SCH is not fully screened for NAT, and occult injuries are found if there is suspicion for abuse and screening is performed [2]. Ophthalmologists are consulted when there is suspicion of NAT, and full indirect ophthalmoscopic examination through a dilated pupil is recommended for the workup of pediatric/infantile SCH in the setting of suspected NAT [3]. When the NAT workup is normal after identifying only a single sentinel injury, it is prudent to analyze the inciting case findings. This idea is even more important when analyzing a finding like SCH, which has multiple etiologies. To our knowledge, there have been no previous reports of SCH associated with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) identified in searches of PubMed and Google Scholar, although pediatric SCH has rarely been associated with other respiratory infections. This observation is noteworthy, given that RSV is the leading cause of lower respiratory tract infections in children [4]. Herein, we present the case of an infant with SCH in the setting of RSV infection whose comprehensive multidisciplinary NAT evaluation identified no evidence of abuse. The aim is to describe a possible illness-associated explanation of the SCH, as this observational case cannot establish causation or rule out abuse. Case Presentation A six-week-old previously healthy female was admitted to the hospital for increased work of breathing and dehydration. She was evaluated in the emergency department (ED) approximately one week earlier for respiratory symptoms, at which time the initial viral panel was negative, and SCH was not specifically evaluated or documented. Supportive care was provided, and she was discharged with return precautions. On subsequent admission approximately one week later, she tested positive for RSV via polymerase chain reaction testing and was found to have SCH of the right eye (Figure 1). The mother, who accompanied the infant through her evaluations, first noticed the SCH during this hospitalization; she did not report a previous history of ocular or facial trauma. No relevant family history was reported. SCH had not been documented at well-child checks or in birth records. As SCH has been recognized as a sentinel injury in young infants and raises concern for possible abuse, a physical exam and multidisciplinary evaluation were initiated. Initial screening measures included computed tomography (CT) of the head, skeletal survey, and dilated funduscopic examination. Laboratory studies were obtained to evaluate for occult injuries or underlying conditions that would predispose to developing SCH (Table 1). Physical examination revealed no other bruises, abrasions, oral injuries, or deformities. Hemoglobin was 9.5 g/dL, a value which the treating pediatric team considered compatible with the physiologic decline in hemoglobin during early infancy. The red blood cell count of 2.67 x10(6)/mcL and hematocrit of 27.4% were similarly considered age-appropriate. The absolute neutrophil count of 1.01 thou/mcL was also considered within age-appropriate limits. An isolated low anion gap of 1 was obtained from a specimen reported to be mildly hemolyzed, with otherwise reassuring electrolyte findings, and was not considered clinically significant. Platelet count and coagulation studies were within the reported reference ranges. The dilated funduscopic examination was grossly normal, with no retinal hemorrhages noted (Table 2). The head CT demonstrated no acute abnormality (Figure 2A). On the initial skeletal survey, the attending pediatric radiologist noted unilaminar periosteal reaction along the femoral and tibial shafts consistent with normal appositional bone growth for age. However, the radiologist considered the medial left proximal tibial metaphyseal spurring “worthy of further evaluation,” stating that “a transmetaphyseal fracture cannot be excluded on this image and further imaging is warranted” (Figure 2C). The concerning finding was seen on the anteroposterior but not the lateral view and was not a confirmed fracture. Child abuse pediatrics was consulted, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, spine, and left knee/tibia was obtained. The MRI of the brain (Figure 2B) and spine was reported as normal, and MRI of the left knee/tibia showed no fracture or associated soft tissue injury (Figure 2D). The skeletal studies were interpreted by attending pediatric radiologists, and MRI studies by attending pediatric neuroradiologists. The Department of Children’s Services (DCS) was contacted and evaluated the home and caregivers involved in the infant’s care. The DCS investigation resulted in no concerns. Respiratory treatment was supportive, no intubation was required, and the infant stabilized on room air. The SCH resolved within one week of admission, and no complications or unexpected adverse events were reported. Following the completed medical and psychosocial evaluation, the infant was discharged to the mother with a planned DCS follow-up home visit and repeat skeletal survey after two weeks. At follow-up, no further injuries were identified, and the proximal tibial finding showed no interval change, favoring physiologic periostitis/metaphyseal spurring rather than fracture (Figure 2E). Discussion Trauma is the most common cause of SCH in young children, but SCH has many other non-traumatic causes, including infectious, inflammatory, hematologic, and vascular conditions [1]. In older children, SCH can occur because of indirect vascular trauma secondary to illnesses that increase forceful Valsalva and intrathoracic pressure, including severe coughing, vomiting, constipation, and sneezing. However, these causative mechanisms are not commonly reported in young infants. Koti et al. found SCH to be extremely rare in children under three years old presenting with cough, vomiting, or constipation [5]. Thus, identifying SCH in a young infant should prompt further investigation for physical abuse, particularly because occult injuries may be identified when appropriate screening is performed [2]. Though RSV is one of the leading viral causes of lower respiratory tract illness in infants [4], there is a paucity of information regarding its ocular sequelae. Previous literature has described SCH in association with other infectious illnesses, including herpes zoster [6], varicella [7,8], pertussis [9], Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection [10], and adenovirus-associated respiratory illness [11]. SCH has also been reported in association with COVID-19 and influenza, although these reports are limited and include neonatal and adult patients [12,13]. Despite these reported associations between SCH and other infectious or respiratory illnesses, we identified no previous report specifically describing SCH in association with RSV infection in searches of PubMed and Google Scholar. It is unlikely that the infant reported in this case had a remaining SCH from delivery, as most birth-associated SCH resolve within the first weeks of life [14]. There were also no concerns for constipation, specific coughing events, or other entities that may have caused forceful Valsalva, despite this being an unlikely cause of SCH in this young age group [5]. Furthermore, spontaneous SCH rarely occurs in children, and its presence should prompt an appropriate workup for other medical causes or traumatic injuries [1]. In this patient, the temporal association between SCH and RSV infection, in the absence of another identified medical or traumatic cause after multidisciplinary evaluation, raises the possibility of an illness-related mechanism. One study reported ocular surface inflammation from conditions such as allergic, viral, neonatal, Kawasaki disease, and Herpes Zoster-related conjunctivitis associated with SCH in 13% of children [1]. We hypothesize that the RSV infectious process may contribute to SCH through mechanisms similar to those proposed for other upper respiratory infections such as COVID and influenza: viral remnants in ocular tissues may cause an inflammatory effect that weakens the blood vessels, allowing for an increased propensity for rupture through the increased intrathoracic pressure that accompanies typical sneezing or coughing in many viral upper respiratory infections [12]. Conjunctivitis has been reported in 11% of children hospitalized with RSV [15]. Whether an ocular inflammatory process contributed to the SCH in this infant cannot be established, and no specific coughing or Valsalva event was documented at its onset. Accordingly, these inflammatory and pressure-related pathways remain biologically plausible hypotheses, rather than established mechanisms, in this patient. SCH in the setting of RSV infection may represent a rare illness-associated finding, and recognizing this possibility could be clinically important given the potentially serious medicolegal consequences of both missed abuse and incorrectly attributed abuse. It is also important to state that child abuse cannot be completely excluded simply because imaging, laboratory studies, and physical examination demonstrated no other injuries; however, physicians should consider other non-traumatic causes, though rare, of SCH in infants in the context of a single sentinel injury with a known medical illness that may contribute to a propensity to develop SCH. The importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis is supported by a 2026 retrospective cohort study in which Tayama et al. found abuse in only 12 (0.9%) of 1,281 infants and young children with SCH [16]. The Tayama et al. cohort included children aged one to <48 months (mean age 22.5 months); isolated SCH was defined as SCH without another injury identified within seven days before or after the SCH, and abuse ascertainment incorporated diagnosis codes with review of clinical notes and radiology reports. These population-level findings do not remove the need for an age-appropriate abuse evaluation in an individual six-week-old infant. Strengths of this case report include the multidisciplinary evaluation with ophthalmic examination, neuroimaging, skeletal surveys, child abuse pediatrics evaluation, and follow-up imaging. These investigations informed the clinical assessment but cannot definitively exclude abuse or establish RSV causation. Limitations of this case report include the inability to establish the exact timing of SCH onset, although SCH was not documented approximately one week prior to admission during the previous ED visit or at well-child checks or in birth records, the lack of previously reported SCH associated with RSV infections, and the impossibility of entirely ruling out abusive trauma as a cause of SCH, despite multidisciplinary evaluation. Additionally, a single case cannot establish a causal relationship between RSV infection and SCH. Nevertheless, the temporal association between RSV infection and the SCH, analogous reports of SCH in association with other respiratory and infectious illnesses, and the absence of another identified explanation for SCH after multidisciplinary evaluation support consideration of RSV-associated illness as a possible explanation. Further study would be necessary to determine whether SCH represents a reproducible, though rare, ocular finding associated with RSV infection. Conclusions SCH in infants is a sentinel finding of non-accidental trauma, raising the concern for child abuse in specific contexts, and should prompt screening for further injuries. While it is virtually impossible to completely exclude inflicted injury in this case, a multidisciplinary team identified no evidence of abuse or additional traumatic injuries. The temporal association of the SCH with RSV infection indicates the possibility of the RSV infectious process contributing to SCH via inflammatory or pressure-related processes associated with respiratory illness, as has been proposed for other infections. This case documents a possible association, not proof of causation. Nonetheless, considering other medical causes for SCH in infants with RSV, after completing a thorough screening for abuse, is as important as accurately diagnosing inflicted injury given potentially serious medicolegal consequences. supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Warning about the burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) on people with chronic diseases. As part of the 2026 Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Awareness Week (November 2-8), GSK – a multinational biopharmaceutical and healthcare company – announced the results of a global survey on the impact of respiratory syncytial virus on adults with chronic diseases. Find Lung Care Hà Nội Mới•07/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 RSV can affect the health and ability to maintain daily activities in people with chronic illnesses. Photo: Vu Thu The survey, commissioned by GSK and conducted online by Human8 (a global strategic consulting and market research organization), took place from July 15 to August 7, 2026, among 6,041 individuals aged 18 and over in 10 countries, including Australia, Brazil, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Poland , Spain, and Taiwan (China). Participants were living with one or more chronic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and hypertension. Read Med Journals Discover more Check Symptoms Find Treatments Study Biology The survey results showed that up to 79% of participants reported that their daily lives were disrupted when they contracted respiratory infections, including RSV. Infections not only cause physical fatigue but also negatively impact mental health, raising anxiety about managing underlying conditions and forcing patients to become more dependent on family care. Worsening of chronic diseases following respiratory viral infections was observed across several groups: 52% in asthma patients, 45% in COPD patients, 35% in chronic kidney disease patients, 29% in cardiovascular disease patients, and 27% in diabetes patients. Additionally, 36% of participants experienced longer-than-expected recovery times, 25% required follow-up visits to their initial healthcare facility, and 18% needed emergency care. Find Lung Care Notably, in the group previously diagnosed with RSV, symptoms and health effects tend to be more persistent. Approximately 55% of those who had RSV self-reported symptoms as moderate or very severe; this rate rose to 68% in patients with chronic kidney disease or COPD, 64% in those with cardiovascular disease, and 63% in those with asthma. You may also like The 2026 RSV Awareness Week aims to help the community better understand RSV and its impact on adults with chronic diseases. Photo: Vu Thu Following the initial infection, 40% of patients reported continued health problems for a month or more, and nearly 10% needed more than a year to recover or were unable to regain their original health. Globally, RSV is a common respiratory infection, estimated to affect around 64 million people annually across all age groups. Find Lung Care RSV virus is increasingly seen as a dangerous cause of respiratory illness in people aged 60 and older. According to epidemiological studies, in 2019 alone, RSV caused approximately 470,000 hospitalizations and 33,000 in-hospital deaths among the elderly in developed countries. In Vietnam, a five-year forecasting model estimates approximately 4.6 million cases of acute respiratory illness caused by RSV in people aged 60 and over, resulting in around 200,000 hospitalizations and 18,000 deaths related to lower respiratory complications. Although 79% of survey participants expressed concern about respiratory viruses interfering with treatment or worsening underlying conditions, there remains a significant gap in public awareness regarding RSV. Nearly half (46%) of people with chronic illnesses had not discussed RSV with healthcare professionals in the past two years, and 33% of patients had never discussed the virus at all. You may also like In light of this situation, Dr. Elena DeAngelis, Medical Director of GSK Vietnam, emphasized that people with chronic diseases need to proactively monitor their health and discuss directly with healthcare professionals about measures to prevent respiratory viral infections, including RSV. The 2026 RSV Awareness Week aims to promote dialogue between the community and professionals, advising people – especially the elderly and those with underlying health conditions – to proactively seek regular check-ups for scientific advice to protect their respiratory health and maintain a long-term quality of life. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 11, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Severe RSV Infections Drive Sharp Short-Term Medical Costs Among Older Japanese Adults by November 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Severe RSV Infections Drive Sharp Short-Term Medical Costs Among Older Japanese Adults Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective cohort study investigating the health and economic burden of medically attended respiratory syncytial virus infections among older adults across Japan has established that the pathogen precipitates substantial, statistically significant short-term increases in healthcare resource utilization and medical expenditures. Drawing information across an observation window spanning 1 September 2008 through 31 August 2021, investigators evaluated records from two prominent administrative repositories: the hospital-based Medical Data Vision claims database and the employer-based JMDC claims database. The research team identified 178 confirmed index events occurring in patients aged 60 years and older between 2009 and 2019, comprising 144 individuals drawn from the hospital-centered Medical Data Vision records and 34 individuals identified within the employment-affiliated JMDC dataset. Across these cohorts, older adults diagnosed with respiratory syncytial virus experienced extensive clinical complications alongside acute escalations in outpatient consultations and hospital admissions, culminating in substantial financial consequences during the initial month following diagnosis that were primarily driven by inpatient hospitalization costs. Respiratory syncytial virus has long been recognized as a leading cause of acute respiratory illness in vulnerable populations, including young pediatric patients and aging adults. In older individuals, particularly those presenting with preexisting cardiovascular diseases, pulmonary conditions, or metabolic disorders like diabetes, infection can progress toward life-threatening manifestations such as severe pneumonia or lower respiratory tract disease, frequently demanding urgent hospitalization or non-invasive mechanical ventilation. Beyond acute primary damage, viral replication can stimulate inflammatory cascades that trigger critical exacerbations of underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchial asthma, and congestive heart failure. Despite these established clinical trajectories, the true epidemiology and financial consequences of respiratory syncytial virus among older demographics in Japan have historically remained underreported. Discover more Biotech startup funding Learn Engineering Track Biotech To rigorously delineate these disease patterns, the researchers examined multi-year datasets capturing inpatient and outpatient health claims across acute-care and commercial insurance networks. The Medical Data Vision repository incorporates anonymized Japanese Diagnosis Procedure Combination records detailing acute-care hospital inpatient care and lump-sum payment systems, containing approximately 45 million patient profiles of which roughly 35 percent represent individuals aged over 65 years. Complementing this acute inpatient framework, the JMDC database compiles health insurance claims from more than 130 payer organizations, encapsulating inpatient admissions, ambulatory encounters, prescription dispensing services, and regular health checkup evaluations across 12 million insured lives, where approximately 2 percent represent adults aged 65 to 74 years. The study protocol mapped distinct twelve-month annual identification cycles running from September through August between 2009 and 2020. This longitudinal architecture required a baseline observation window spanning 365 days prior to the first confirmed diagnostic claim alongside a structured follow-up monitoring period after the index viral infection. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales Laboratory equipment supplier Case qualification required patients aged 60 years or older to demonstrate at least one documented medical claim carrying a specific Tenth Revision International Statistical Classification of Diseases code indicative of respiratory syncytial virus infection, encompassing diagnostic classifications B34.8, J12.1, J20.5, or J21.0. Because administrative datasets lack explicit laboratory confirmation dates, index diagnosis dates were established through systematic database-specific algorithms integrating treatment initiation markers, hospital admission records, service delivery timelines, and monthly claims submissions. Within the Medical Data Vision cohort, the mean patient age was 74.5 years with a standard deviation of 9.1 years, and 58 percent of these individuals received medical management in tertiary medical centers containing more than 500 beds. Within the JMDC cohort, which was restricted by database coverage to individuals aged 60 to 74 years, the mean age stood at 64.0 years with a standard deviation of 3.6 years, and 47 percent were evaluated within smaller medical clinics maintaining fewer than 20 beds. Across the entire 2009 through 2019 timeline, the overall documented incidence rate within the Medical Data Vision cohort was calculated at 0.007 per 1,000 person-years. Preexisting medical comorbidities were documented during the 365-day baseline window, revealing that 93 to 94 percent of patients presented with chronic underlying disorders prior to acquiring their viral infection. The overall burden of baseline illness differed markedly between the study populations, reflecting the distinct structural characteristics of each database. The median modified Charlson comorbidity index reached 5 in the hospital-based Medical Data Vision cohort compared to 1 in the younger, employment-based JMDC population. The most prevalent baseline comorbidities recorded across the study cohorts included type 2 diabetes, congestive heart failure, systemic hypertension, solid malignant tumors, chronic liver failure, bronchial asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Every identified patient demonstrated concurrent manifestations of lower respiratory tract disease, upper respiratory tract disease, or both during their primary episode. Lower respiratory tract conditions were identified in 78.5 percent of Medical Data Vision patients and 58.8 percent of JMDC patients, confirming that medically attended presentations in older Japanese adults predominantly involve deep pulmonary pathology. Acute clinical complications arising between seven days prior to the index diagnosis date and fourteen days following diagnosis were exceptionally frequent, occurring in 61.1 percent of the Medical Data Vision cohort and 55.9 percent of the JMDC cohort. Documented secondary clinical events included acute congestive heart failure decompensation, bacterial and viral pneumonia, acute bronchitis, and acute respiratory failure. Among individuals possessing a documented baseline history of bronchial asthma, acute disease exacerbations occurred in 25.0 percent of the Medical Data Vision group and 20.0 percent of the JMDC group. Furthermore, among Medical Data Vision patients with preexisting chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, 18.8 percent suffered acute pulmonary exacerbations during their infection, whereas no such exacerbations were cataloged within the smaller JMDC cohort. Therapeutic interventions reflected this clinical severity, with diagnostic chest radiography and therapeutic oxygen inhalation emerging as the two most frequently administered procedures, both displaying statistically significant post-diagnosis utilization increases across all evaluated intervals. Evaluation of healthcare resource utilization demonstrated marked, statistically significant increases when comparing the acute 30-day post-diagnosis window against the average 30-day baseline consumption derived across the preceding pre-event year. Within the Medical Data Vision cohort, the average number of outpatient consultations per patient rose from a baseline mean of 1.21 visits to 2.07 visits in the post-event timeframe, representing a statistically significant escalation supported by paired sample testing. Concurrently, the average frequency of inpatient hospitalizations increased more than fivefold, rising from a baseline mean of 0.07 admissions per individual to 0.37 admissions during the acute month following diagnosis. Similar patterns appeared in the JMDC cohort, where outpatient encounters exhibited an average increase of 1.44 visits per patient, moving from 2.15 baseline visits to 3.59 visits during the acute post-event interval. These spikes in hospitalizations and outpatient attendances subsided across subsequent observation windows of 180 and 365 days, indicating that acute healthcare operational pressures normalize toward baseline values once the acute viral infection resolves. The economic burden accompanying these heightened medical interventions was substantial, with the Medical Data Vision cohort demonstrating a statistically significant average cost increase of 196,231.7 Japanese yen per patient during the initial 30 days post-diagnosis. Mean healthcare spending surged from a 30-day pre-event baseline of 132,109.7 yen to 328,341.4 yen post-diagnosis. Inpatient hospital admissions served as the dominant economic driver, contributing an additional 187,256.0 yen in hospital lodging and acute therapeutic fees as inpatient costs expanded from 89,544.9 yen to 276,800.9 yen. Subgroup stratification illustrated that financial consequences scaled directly with advancing patient age. Individuals aged 60 to 74 years incurred an average cost rise of 122,552.2 yen, whereas patients aged 75 years and older experienced an average expenditure surge of 280,908.1 yen, of which 270,903.9 yen stemmed entirely from inpatient hospitalization expenses. Clinical stratification further revealed that patients presenting with lower respiratory tract disease experienced a mean cost surge of 234,250.6 yen driven by hospital admissions, while patients exhibiting isolated upper respiratory tract involvement experienced a non-significant cost change of 57,646.7 yen. Preexisting medical vulnerability heavily influenced incremental expenditure profiles across comorbidity subgroups within the hospital-based population. Similarly, patients diagnosed with baseline cardiovascular disorders recorded an overall expenditure increase of 267,994.7 yen, predominantly governed by a 264,880.7 yen expansion in hospital inpatient care. Subgroups with diagnosed type 2 diabetes and chronic pulmonary conditions generated incremental cost burdens of 175,618.8 yen and 150,362.9 yen, respectively, with inpatient diabetes admissions accounting for 171,005.5 yen of that group’s expenditure surge. Hospitalization frequencies expanded across all comorbidity cohorts, increasing by an average of 0.39 admissions per patient among cardiovascular cases, 0.30 among diabetic cases, 0.28 among renal failure cases, and 0.26 among patients with chronic pulmonary disease, confirming that underlying organ dysfunction amplifies inpatient admission risks during acute infection. The study authors highlighted several methodological considerations that contextualize their findings and delineate clear boundaries for clinical interpretation. Because the Medical Data Vision dataset exclusively captures hospital-based claims, it inherently samples an older population displaying heightened clinical acuity, meaning that observed utilization rates and monetary costs cannot be generalized directly to mild or unmanaged community infections. Furthermore, the mandatory requirement that Medical Data Vision participants maintain continuous claims every six months across baseline and follow-up intervals may have excluded individuals with milder illness who did not seek routine healthcare, potentially overestimating per-patient burden while underestimating overall population infection volumes. Administrative coding limitations, reliance on indirect diagnostic estimation algorithms rather than exact clinical testing timestamps, single-event indexing per annual cycle, and potential coding overlap across nonspecific lower respiratory categories also represent analytical constraints. Nevertheless, by demonstrating significant short-term cost spikes and severe acute complications among hospitalized older adults, these real-world findings provide critical baseline evidence to inform future clinical management, diagnostic vigilance, and targeted vaccination initiatives across Japan.
