supplementary_news.content_title: Health officials see sharp increase of flu and RSV cases in children
supplementary_news.content: TEXAS — Chances are, you know someone who is sick or recovering from an illness. Health officials say there’s been a sharp increase in influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) cases in children. Within the state of Texas, there’s been an increase in flu cases, particularly influenza A, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data and local health officials. The Texas Department of State Health Services started reporting flu cases at the beginning of October, and according to its Respiratory Illness Interactive Dashboard , flu and RSV cases are still high. Texas hospitals and urgent care centers are seeing more children who have the flu every day, but Dr. Natalie Tarrant from Texas Children’s Hospital said we haven’t even seen the peak of flu season yet. “Definitely started earlier than you asked last year. And we don’t know if that means that flu season will just be shifted, where the whole thing starts earlier and ends earlier, or if that means that it’s just going to be a worse year than last year. Last year was worse than the average year for flu,” Tarrant said. But when should you take your child to see a doctor? Dr. Suzanne Whitworth from Cook Children’s Hospital said that, when it comes to children, you have to trust your gut. “Any time you have anxiety and your radar goes off, that you need to see a doctor, call. Either call one or go to urgent care. For sure, you want to go see a doctor if there is any difficulty breathing,” Whitworth said. Dr. Whitworth said a fever can also indicate if your child is very ill. “For healthy, normal children, fever is anything that's a 100.4 or higher rectally. And so if your child has significant fever and they’re not acting right and not feeling okay or dehydrated or not feeling well, that’s another reason to give your doctor a call,” she said. According to Dr. Tarrant, the best way to protect your children from the flu is prevention, and she recommends parents get their children the flu shot. “Vaccination is key. It’s it’s really exciting... as a pediatrician, a new vaccine comes out that changes the landscape of what we see in the office,” Tarrant said. “And the RSV vaccine has been amazing for us. Flu vaccine, we always recommend universally for everybody, but especially the babies, because the babies have a lot of trouble with flu.”

supplementary_news.content_title: Children’s Mercy Kansas City Will Keep Kids Under 13 Off Its Inpatient Units Starting Nov. 10 as RSV and Flu Season Builds
supplementary_news.content: Sun, November 8, 2026 at 8:30 PM UTC Tuesday, Nov. 10, is the day the youngest visitors lose their place at the bedside at Children’s Mercy Kansas City. From that date, children 12 and under, which means every child under 13, will not be allowed on the hospital’s inpatient units, a rule the hospital says is tied to respiratory virus season, which includes RSV, flu and COVID-19. The rule was announced in an Oct. 22 post on the hospital’s Parent-ish blog by pediatric infectious disease physicians Dr. Edward R. Lyon and Dr. Christelle M. Ilboudo. The hospital’s visitor pages, updated Nov. 6, spell out who is affected and who is not. Who Can and Cannot Come Up to the Inpatient Floors According to the hospital’s visitor guidelines , children 12 and under “will not be able to visit patients in the hospital” once the viral season rules begin. Visitors ages 13 to 16 may come, but they must always be with an adult. All visitors must feel well and be free of illness. Parents and guardians are treated differently. The hospital’s visiting hours page says they are part of the care team rather than visitors, and they may be with their child around the clock. They receive a green wristband, must sign in and have to follow all safety precautions. Up to two parents, guardians or authorized adults may stay overnight in the patient’s room. Other guests may visit from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Visitors 16 and older need a driver’s license or other photo ID and must wear the sticker they are given. The page notes that exceptions are sometimes possible and tells families to ask their child’s nurse. The restrictions do not apply to clinic or outpatient visits. A family whose child is admitted after a clinic or emergency room visit does face a practical problem, though. According to the hospital, brothers and sisters 12 and under who came along cannot go up to the inpatient unit, so families are told to plan for another caregiver for those children. Why the Cutoff Falls at Age 12 Children’s Mercy says the reasoning is about both risk and habits. The hospital’s visiting hours page states that children 12 and under are the most likely to catch these viruses and the least likely to follow the habits that stop them from spreading. The Parent-ish post puts it more briefly: children 12 and under are the most at risk of catching a virus. Ilboudo is quoted on the visitor guidelines page making the broader point: “Anyone who has a respiratory virus can give it to someone else.” The hospital says the rules protect sick children, their families and staff. The post describes how the viruses move. RSV spreads through respiratory droplets or when a person touches a contaminated surface and then touches the face. Influenza also travels in droplets and, the doctors write, can last at least a week and can be deadly, so it should not be dismissed as “not that bad.” The hospital’s visitor pages add that the policy can change during periods of high infection risk. The timing lines up with the calendar. The CDC says on its RSV page that RSV spreads in fall and winter and usually peaks in December and January. What the CDC and Children’s Mercy Say About RSV and Flu in Young Children The Children’s Mercy doctors write that RSV is the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the U.S., and that most hospitalized infants had no chronic medical problems. The American Academy of Pediatrics makes a similar point on its RSV campaign page , calling RSV the most common cause of hospitalization in children under age 1. For most healthy children RSV looks like a cold. The Parent-ish post says it usually clears in one to two weeks but can cause bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants under 6 months and in children with weakened immune systems. The CDC’s page on RSV symptoms says very young infants may show only irritability, decreased activity and breathing difficulties. Symptoms usually appear four to six days after infection and tend to develop in stages. The CDC advises calling a health care professional if a child has difficulty breathing, is not drinking enough fluids or is getting worse, and it says aspirin should not be given to children. Flu carries its own numbers. The CDC’s page on flu in children estimates 6,000 to 25,000 flu-related hospitalizations a year among children under 5. Annual vaccination is recommended for everyone 6 months and older, and children 6 months through 8 years need two doses if it is their first vaccination, if they have had only one previous dose or if their history is unknown. The second dose comes at least four weeks after the first. The Children’s Mercy doctors say not to delay the flu shot while waiting for a particular type. For babies, the post lists two one-time antibody injections that are not vaccines: nirsevimab (Beyfortus) for infants entering their first RSV season, and clesrovimab (Enflonsia) for infants under 1. It also names Abrysvo, an RSV vaccine given during pregnancy so mothers pass antibodies to the baby. Parents are told to ask their child’s doctor about eligibility. An earlier Parent Diaries report on RSV in babies under 6 months covers how symptoms tend to progress. The CDC’s list of flu emergency warning signs for children includes fast or difficult breathing, bluish lips or face, ribs pulling inward with each breath, dehydration, a child who is not alert, seizures and a fever above 104 degrees that does not respond to medicine. It also lists any fever in a child younger than 12 weeks. Get stories like this by email. Sign up for The Parent Diaries Letter . The investigation, published as a brief research report in Frontiers in Public Health, evaluated 438 participants and identified fourteen positive individuals, yielding an estimated prevalence with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 1.8 to 5.3 percent. Respiratory viruses remain a primary global public health concern and represent leading causes of acute respiratory infections worldwide. University students represent a potentially important group for viral circulation because of frequent social interaction. Evidence regarding respiratory virus circulation in university populations from Latin America remains limited. Discover more Healthcare Tour Colleges infections To evaluate viral prevalence and examine the proportion of infections among individuals without symptoms, researchers gathered a convenience sample of healthcare students between January 4 and February 3, 2026. The multicenter study was conducted among healthcare university students from universities located in Quito, Guayaquil, and Cuenca, Ecuador. Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms View Census Data Get Health Tips Diagnostic evaluations were conducted on site by collecting nasopharyngeal samples and analyzing them with a combo rapid antigen point-of-care test designed to detect respiratory syncytial virus, Influenza A, Influenza B, and Adenovirus. In parallel with antigen testing, investigators systematically recorded sociodemographic and epidemiological variables. Among the fourteen students who tested positive for at least one respiratory pathogen, Influenza A virus and respiratory syncytial virus were the most frequently observed single detections, each identified in four participants. Adenovirus was confirmed as a single detection in three participants, and the authors documented three cases of viral coinfection within the positive group. Clinical symptom tracking revealed that eight of the fourteen positive participants, representing 57.1 percent, were asymptomatic at testing, while six participants, or 42.9 percent, reported experiencing respiratory symptoms. The analysis revealed a statistically significant association between the presence of respiratory symptoms and viral detection, with an observed significance level of p less than 0.001. The authors observed that because more than half of the infected students exhibited no symptoms, respiratory viruses may circulate unnoticed within university settings. The study concluded that overall respiratory virus detection was low in this cohort and demonstrated that rapid antigen tests are operationally feasible point-of-care tools for on-site screening in academic environments. supplementary_news.content_title: Medical Societies Back New Respiratory Vaccine Guidance
supplementary_news.content: RESPIRATORY vaccine guidance has gained unified support from four leading medical societies ahead of the 2026–2027 virus season. The American Thoracic Society (ATS), American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (AAAAI), American College of Chest Physicians (CHEST), and Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) have unanimously endorsed recommendations for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and COVID-19 vaccination in adults and children. The joint endorsement aims to provide consistent, evidence-based recommendations for clinicians managing patients with respiratory conditions, particularly those vulnerable to severe viral illness. The multisociety Vaccine Guidance Review Panel was established following changes to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) processes in 2025. According to the participating organizations, these changes resulted in potentially harmful modifications to vaccination schedules, raising concerns about consistency with established scientific evidence. In response, the panel reviewed and endorsed the vaccine recommendation development processes and resulting guidance from four medical organizations: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Infectious Diseases Society of America. The panel also reached consensus on guidance aligned with ACIP recommendations issued before June 2025, reinforcing a coordinated approach to respiratory disease prevention. The endorsement covers influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 vaccination recommendations across pediatric and adult populations. A particular priority is ensuring that clinicians caring for patients with chronic or acute respiratory diseases have access to consistent vaccination guidance as seasonal respiratory virus circulation increases. The organizations emphasized that preventive vaccination remains an essential component of protecting patients against severe respiratory illness. Michelle Ng Gong, ATS President, highlighted the importance of clear recommendations for clinicians treating patients with serious lung disease, particularly during periods of uncertainty surrounding national vaccination policies. For physicians, the endorsement establishes a unified professional position on respiratory vaccination and provides a framework for discussing preventive care with patients. The participating societies emphasized that consistent recommendations can strengthen clinical decision-making, support patient education, and promote equitable access to preventive healthcare. The collaboration also reinforces the importance of integrating vaccination into routine respiratory and critical care, particularly for populations at greatest risk of severe illness. By aligning recommendations across specialties, the panel aims to reduce confusion and strengthen confidence in evidence-based vaccination ahead of the respiratory virus season. The investigation, published as a brief research report in Frontiers in Public Health, evaluated 438 participants and identified fourteen positive individuals, yielding an estimated prevalence with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 1.8 to 5.3 percent. Respiratory viruses remain a primary global public health concern and represent leading causes of acute respiratory infections worldwide. University students represent a potentially important group for viral circulation because of frequent social interaction. Evidence regarding respiratory virus circulation in university populations from Latin America remains limited. To evaluate viral prevalence and examine the proportion of infections among individuals without symptoms, researchers gathered a convenience sample of healthcare students between January 4 and February 3, 2026. The multicenter study was conducted among healthcare university students from universities located in Quito, Guayaquil, and Cuenca, Ecuador. Diagnostic evaluations were conducted on site by collecting nasopharyngeal samples and analyzing them with a combo rapid antigen point-of-care test designed to detect respiratory syncytial virus, Influenza A, Influenza B, and Adenovirus. In parallel with antigen testing, investigators systematically recorded sociodemographic and epidemiological variables. Among the fourteen students who tested positive for at least one respiratory pathogen, Influenza A virus and respiratory syncytial virus were the most frequently observed single detections, each identified in four participants. Adenovirus was confirmed as a single detection in three participants, and the authors documented three cases of viral coinfection within the positive group. Clinical symptom tracking revealed that eight of the fourteen positive participants, representing 57.1 percent, were asymptomatic at testing, while six participants, or 42.9 percent, reported experiencing respiratory symptoms. The analysis revealed a statistically significant association between the presence of respiratory symptoms and viral detection, with an observed significance level of p less than 0.001. The authors observed that because more than half of the infected students exhibited no symptoms, respiratory viruses may circulate unnoticed within university settings. The study concluded that overall respiratory virus detection was low in this cohort and demonstrated that rapid antigen tests are operationally feasible point-of-care tools for on-site screening in academic environments. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 11, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology AAPR ratio shows modest link to bacterial type in pediatric RSV by November 10, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 AAPR ratio shows modest link to bacterial type in pediatric RSV Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective study published in BMC Microbiology has identified a potential association between the Albumin-to-Alkaline Phosphatase Ratio, known as AAPR, and the specific type of bacterial co-infection in children suffering from respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV. The study focused on 153 children with laboratory-confirmed RSV who also had bacterial co-infections, aiming to evaluate the discriminative performance of AAPR and explore relevant biological pathways. RSV infection in children is frequently complicated by bacterial co-infection, a condition that significantly aggravates clinical outcomes. The AAPR has recently emerged as a novel marker in this field, prompting the researchers to investigate its utility. The primary objective was to determine the association between AAPR levels and the phenotypes of Gram-positive versus Gram-negative bacterial co-infection. By analyzing this specific cohort, the study sought to provide insights into the underlying biological mechanisms that might link these metabolic markers to infection types. The study employed a retrospective design, analyzing data from 153 pediatric patients. To determine the independent association and dose-response relationship between AAPR and infection phenotypes, the researchers utilized multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline analyses. Diagnostic performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, or AUC. Additionally, an exploratory systems biology analysis was performed to identify candidate genes and signaling pathways potentially relevant to the observed association. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales Laboratory equipment supplier Biotech startup funding The multivariable logistic regression results demonstrated that elevated AAPR was independently and inversely associated with the likelihood of Gram-positive infection. Specifically, the odds ratio was 0.37, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.15 to 0.89 for the highest versus the lowest tertile. This suggests that children with higher AAPR values were less likely to have Gram-positive bacterial co-infections compared to those with lower values. The restricted cubic spline analysis showed no evidence of a nonlinear association, with a P value for non-linearity of 0.456. The association remained similar after nonlinear adjustment for age and was directionally consistent across age strata. However, the relationship was attenuated after normalization using age-specific pediatric alkaline phosphatase reference limits. This indicates that while the association is present, its strength may be influenced by age-related variations in alkaline phosphatase levels. The researchers noted that the inverse association with Gram-positive infection was a key finding, highlighting the potential role of AAPR in differentiating bacterial types. In terms of diagnostic performance, AAPR alone showed modest discriminative performance, with an AUC of 0.599. When AAPR was added to other standard markers such as C-reactive protein, white blood cell count, and neutrophil count, the AUC increased from 0.455 to 0.613. However, this improvement did not reach the conventional threshold for statistical significance, with a P value of 0.051. This suggests that while AAPR may add some value to existing diagnostic panels, it is not yet a standalone tool for distinguishing between bacterial co-infection types. The exploratory systems biology analysis identified several inflammation-related pathways as candidates for further investigation. These included the interleukin-17, tumor necrosis factor, and other pathways involved in immune responses. The identification of these pathways provides a potential biological basis for the observed association between AAPR and bacterial co-infection phenotypes. Further research is needed to confirm these pathways and understand their specific roles in the context of RSV and bacterial co-infections. Discover more Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Donate to Research Find Study Aids The study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. The retrospective design and the relatively small sample size of 153 patients may limit the generalizability of the findings. The modest discriminative performance of AAPR alone and the lack of statistical significance when added to other markers indicate that more research is needed to validate its clinical utility. Despite these limitations, the study provides valuable insights into the potential role of AAPR as an immuno-metabolic marker in pediatric RSV infections. The inverse association with Gram-positive bacterial co-infection and the identification of relevant inflammation pathways offer promising avenues for future research. supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content Main navigation Top stories Health Crime Politics Business Tech Culture Sports Weird 1-1-2 Top stories Health Crime Politics Business Tech Culture Sports Weird 1-1-2 Image Cropped view of doctor in latex gloves holding syringe and vaccine on blurred foreground near patient - Credit: IgorVetushko / DepositPhotos - License: DepositPhotos Health RSV vaccination Ikazia Hospital Rotterdam COPD Zorginstituut Nederland covid-19 pandemic » More tags « Less tags Share this article: Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Elderly people also vulnerable to RS virus; Doctors call for vaccinations Friday, 6 November 2026 - 21:10 The respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), commonly associated with serious infections in babies and young children, also poses a significant health risk to older people, particularly those with chronic lung and heart conditions, Dutch lung specialists have said to NOS. They are calling for vulnerable elderly people to receive RSV vaccinations to prevent serious illness and hospital admissions. However, there is a disagreement over who should pay for the vaccines. The Dutch healthcare reimbursement authority, Zorginstituut Nederland, has not yet recommended including them in the basic health insurance package. It expects to issue a new assessment in early 2027. RSV is a common winter virus, and infections among older people can have serious consequences, including pneumonia, hospitalisation and death. One of the doctors featured in the report is Chantal Kroesse, a pulmonologist at Ikazia Hospital in Rotterdam. “We know better now. During the Covid-19 pandemic, a rapid test became available that allowed us to test for influenza, Covid-19 and RSV simultaneously. That was when we immediately began to see the impact of the virus." Kroesse has been pushing for better protection for patients with chronic lung conditions. The pulmonologist managed to convince a health insurer to reimburse RSV vaccinations for vulnerable patients. This quickly led to the number of RSV hospital admissions among the relevant patient group falling from 95 to 34, a reduction of 64 percent. She argues that vaccinating vulnerable patients is also worthwhile because the costs of hospital admissions are considerably higher than those of vaccination. "One vaccination can help prevent a serious infection and hospital admission. Do the maths. A vaccine costs around 200 euros, while a hospital admission can easily cost thousands." RSV stands for respiratory syncytial virus. It is a highly contagious virus that causes infections of the respiratory tract. It is particularly well known in the Netherlands because almost all children contract it before their second birthday. In babies, it can cause serious respiratory problems, including bronchiolitis and pneumonia. The Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) specifically identifies older people, people with heart or lung conditions, and those with weakened immune systems as groups at increased risk. A study published last week identified 97,279 hospital admissions for acute respiratory infections among 63,420 patients aged 50 and older. The estimated annual rate of RSV-related respiratory infection admissions was 0.70 per 1,000 people among those aged 50 and older. Among people aged 75 and older, that figure increased to 1.92 per 1,000. During peak months, RSV accounted for up to 30 percent of hospital admissions for acute respiratory infections, with patients staying in hospital for an average of seven to eight days. "An RSV infection can become much more than just a few days of having a cold for someone with COPD,” Kroesse said. "The infection can put such a strain on the lungs that someone needs additional oxygen or has to be admitted to hospital."
